props.title: Ronald Read versus Richard Fuscone

left.name: Ronald Read
lines: Janitor and gas-station attendant; first in family to finish high school; hitchhiked to campus.
Bought a two-bedroom house for $12,000 at age 38 and lived there for life.
Widowed at 50; hobby: chopping firewood. Died 2014, age 92.
Estate more than $8 million: $2 million to family, more than $6 million to hospital and library.
No lottery, no inheritance: saved what he could, bought blue-chip stocks, waited decades.

right.name: Richard Fuscone
lines: Harvard M.B.A.; Merrill Lynch executive; retired in his 40s; Crain's 40 under 40.
Expanded an 18,000-square-foot Greenwich home: 11 bathrooms, 2 elevators, 2 pools, 7 garages.
Cost more than $90,000 a month to maintain. Then 2008 hit.
Told a bankruptcy judge in 2008: 'I currently have no income.' Palm Beach house foreclosed.
2014 Greenwich foreclosure: sold 75% below the insurer's figure — five months before Read's gifts.

props.note: Book-dated stories, 2020 text. Not a forecast.

rows.v: A janitor with no degree can outperform a Harvard-trained executive in investing.
A janitor will not outperform a Harvard surgeon, architect, or nuclear engineer.
Luck independent of skill — or behaviour mattering more than technical knowledge.
Financial success is mostly a soft skill: how you behave is more important than what you know.
2,813,503 Americans died in 2014; fewer than 4,000 left a net worth over $8 million. Read was one.
